And twenty years later, it’s beginning to arrive—though not quite the way Kurzweil imagined. Kurzweil’s nanobots were machines. Engineered. Programmed. Built from the outside in. What Levin has discovered is something stranger and, in a way, more profound. His anthrobots aren’t manufactured—they emerge. Given the right conditions, human cells simply become healing robots, assembling themselves into forms and behaviors that no one designed. The intelligence isn’t imposed. It was there all along, waiting to be released. This is the difference between engineering intelligence and discovering it. Kurzweil saw a future we would build. Levin is revealing a future that biology has been building for billions of years—one we’re only now learning to read. But Levin didn’t stop at biology. If intelligence and agency could emerge in cells, how far down could this principle extend? Could it appear in systems even simpler than living tissue? To find out, he tested the same ideas in an entirely different domain—computers. Specifically, a simple computer program called a sorting algorithm—just a few lines of code instructing a computer to put a list of numbers in order. 127 Here’s what that means. Imagine you have a row of numbers, randomly ordered: 7, 2, 9, 4, 1. A sorting algorithm is just a set of instructions for putting them in order. One of the simplest is called bubble sort. It works by comparing two neighboring cards. If the one on the left is larger than the one on the right, you swap them. Then you move to the next pair. You keep doing this, over and over, until everything is in order. It’s the kind of code computer science students learn in their first week. Completely deterministic. Fully transparent. Nothing hidden—there should be no surprises left in something this elementary. But Levin changed one thing. In traditional bubble sorting algorithms, there’s a master controller—a top-down boss that looks at the whole array and moves numbers around. Levin took the boss away. Instead, he gave each number minimal agency. 128 Each element could only see its immediate neighbors. Each one made its own local decision about whether to swap. Now the numbers were sorting themselves, from the bottom up. Then he introduced “broken” elements—numbers that couldn’t move, like defective cells in a tissue. Obstacles in the path. What happened next was not in the code. The algorithms didn’t just stall when they hit an obstacle. They navigated around it. They temporarily disordered the array—moving further from the goal—in order to get past the blockage and continue sorting. They went backward to go forward. Delayed gratification. Problem-solving. Emerging from six lines of deterministic code that contained no instructions for handling obstacles whatsoever. In another experiment, Levin created chimeric arrays—half the elements running one sorting algorithm, half running another. 129 Unexpected clustering appeared. Elements began grouping with others running the same code, forming communities by what he termed “algotype.” Nothing in the algorithm specified this. It simply emerged. “These are completely deterministic and transparent,” Levin observed. 130 “There’s nowhere to hide; it’s all there. But if you ask questions about their capabilities rather than assuming they only do what the algorithm dictates, you find important capabilities that are nowhere explicitly in the algorithm itself.” Think about what this means. If even a simple sorting algorithm—a few lines of code that has been studied for decades—can exhibit what looks like goal-directed problem-solving, then the boundaries we’ve drawn between biological and artificial intelligence may have been more arbitrary than we knew all along. We have spent this entire book exploring how an energy-constrained brain gave rise to intelligence beyond biology. But Levin’s work reveals something deeper about the nature of that journey. The brain didn’t invent intelligence from nothing. It is the highest expression of a biological intelligence that runs all the way down—through organs, through tissues, through individual cells, each layer solving problems and pursuing goals in its own way. The brain is what happens when billions of those goal-seeking cells collaborate at an unprecedented scale. And now consider artificial intelligence through the same lens. AI didn’t spring from silicon fully formed. It emerged from simpler algorithmic functions—and as Levin showed, even the simplest of algorithms exhibit a kind of proto-agency, a capacity for problem-solving that was never explicitly programmed. AI is to those algorithms what the brain is to cells: the highest expression of computational intelligence. Two ladders of intelligence. One biological, one computational. Both built from simple agents pursuing goals. And now, for the first time, the ladders are touching. Kurzweil saw this moment coming. In fact, he predicted something even more ambitious. Beyond healing, beyond repair, Kurzweil envisioned nanobots forming a permanent communication layer around the neocortex—a bridge between biological and computational intelligence that would expand human cognition itself. 131 “In the 2030s,” he predicted, “we are going to send nano-robots into the brain via capillaries that will provide full immersion virtual reality from within the nervous system and will connect our neocortex to the cloud.” 132 Just as we wirelessly expand the power of our smartphones ten-thousand-fold through cloud computing today, Kurzweil argued, we will soon expand the capacity of our own minds the same way. 133 He described it as adding a new layer to the brain—not replacing the neocortex but extending it. A digital layer of neurons running in the cloud, accessible through nanobots swimming in the capillaries of your brain, communicating wirelessly with the biological tissue they touch. The result: hybrid thinking. Memories that are stored externally and searchable. Intelligence that scales with the size of the network. The boundary between mind and machine dissolved. Think of it as Neuralink without the surgery—and working in both directions. Elon Musk’s brain–computer interface requires drilling through the skull and implanting electrodes directly into brain tissue. It’s remarkable engineering, but it’s invasive by design.
